title: National Manufacturing Day, 2025
summary:
The proclamation marks National Manufacturing Day by celebrating American factories and workers, and by outlining the administration’s plan to grow production at home through tariffs, deregulation, tax incentives, and new technology.

It highlights claims of more than $5 trillion in new investment commitments and 450,000 new jobs early in the term. The approach centers on placing tariffs on some imports to shield U.S. producers, with the stated goal of investing the tariff revenue back into communities. It also promises to remove rules the administration views as barriers to growth, roll back certain climate-focused policies, and offer full, upfront tax write-offs for building or upgrading factories. A push to use artificial intelligence and expand workforce training is presented as a way to raise productivity and help workers transition as industries modernize. The message is clear: strengthen domestic industry, bring capital home, and make it easier and faster to build.

Who stands to benefit? U.S. manufacturers, suppliers, and construction firms that build plants could see more orders and hiring. Towns with a manufacturing base may gain jobs and tax dollars. Companies planning major industrial projects may benefit from faster approvals and immediate tax write-offs. Workers in trades and advanced manufacturing could find more opportunities, especially with added training.

Who might be negatively affected? Businesses that rely on imported parts or goods may face higher costs, which can mean higher prices for consumers. Exporters could be exposed if trading partners respond with their own tariffs. Rolling back environmental rules could worry groups focused on health, climate, and long-term sustainability. Immediate tax write-offs may reduce government revenue in the short term. And as factories adopt more automation, some jobs could shift or disappear without effective retraining.

The proclamation closes by inviting Americans to recognize the entrepreneurs, innovators, and workers who keep the country’s industrial engine running.
